subject.title: RFC: Standard Hosting Profiles and Ready Check

question: Should OpenClaw core promote its existing readiness and configuration facts into named, release-tested hosting-profile contracts, and should acceptance begin with only the canonical local foundation or the full four-profile matrix?
rationale: The code has suitable extension seams and the RFC is coherent, but choosing which runtime shapes become stable core support promises—and which existing users may begin failing readiness—requires maintainer intent.

options.title: Accept the local foundation
options.body: Approve the canonical condition/result schema and backward-compatible local projection first, with separate later decisions for container, reverse-proxy, node-mode, and blocking release gates.

options.title: Accept the full matrix
options.body: Approve all four built-in profiles, strict selection rules, node-mode predicates, and package-acceptance release gating as one support contract.

options.title: Retain unprofiled readiness
options.body: Keep current core readiness facts but leave hosting-shape validation and support matrices to downstream hosts or optional tooling.

recommendation.title: Accept the local foundation
recommendation.body: Approve the canonical condition/result schema and backward-compatible local projection first, with separate later decisions for container, reverse-proxy, node-mode, and blocking release gates.

likelyOwner.reason: The central public probe behavior and its security and redaction boundary trace to his implementation, making him the strongest available owner for deciding whether that surface becomes a broader hosting contract.
